name: Maple-Dijon Pork Tenderloin with Roasted Apples
description: Pork tenderloin seared and roasted with apples in a maple-dijon glaze, served with mashed sweet potatoes and crispy brussels sprouts.
ingredients: 2 firm apples (Cosmic Crisp works well), cored and cut into thick wedges
1 lb brussels sprouts, trimmed and halved
2 lb sweet potatoes, peeled and cubed
instructions: Heat the oven to 425°F. Whisk the dijon, maple syrup, and cider vinegar in a small bowl and set aside.
Put the sweet potatoes in a large pot, cover with cold water, add a big pinch of salt, and bring to a boil. Simmer about 20 minutes, until a fork slides through easily.
Toss the brussels sprouts with 1 Tbsp olive oil, salt, and pepper on a sheet pan. Spread cut-side down in a single layer — that contact is what makes them crispy.
Pat the pork dry and season all over with salt and pepper. Heat the remaining olive oil in an oven-safe skillet over medium-high and sear on all sides until deeply browned, about 6 minutes total.
Scatter the apples and thyme around the pork. Brush half the glaze over the pork. Put the skillet and the brussels sheet pan in the oven together.
Roast until the pork hits 145°F at the thickest point, about 15–18 minutes, brushing with the rest of the glaze halfway through. Start checking at 15 minutes — thin tenderloins cook fast.
Pull the brussels at about 22 minutes, when the outer leaves are dark and crisp and the cut sides are browned.
Drain the sweet potatoes and return to the hot pot for a minute to steam off. Mash with butter, milk, cinnamon, and salt to taste.
Move the pork to a board and rest 10 minutes before slicing. Leave the apples in the skillet to soak up the pan glaze.
Slice into medallions, spoon the apples and pan juices over the top, and serve with the mash and brussels.
tips: The pork is done at 145°F — pull it even if it looks slightly pink inside. That's the single thing that decides whether tenderloin is juicy or dry.
The sweet potatoes can be boiled and mashed earlier in the day and reheated with a splash of milk. The brussels are the one thing that should go straight from oven to table.
Firm apples hold their shape in the skillet; softer varieties turn to sauce.
